#24426. Industry News: Exercised, Rarely Recovered: What Public Reports Say About Recovery in 50 AI Agent Harnesses and Runtimes

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (195 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Exercised, Rarely Recovered: What Public Reports Say About Recovery in 50 AI Agent Harnesses and Runtimes

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (195 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.27090v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When an AI coding agent deletes the wrong files or a long agent run crashes, people fall back on recovery mechanisms: resume from a checkpoint, undo, ask for approval, read the log. Research runtimes promise stronger guarantees, such as saga-style compensation and transactional rollback. We ask what public evidence reveals about whether either kind works in real use. Under a protocol frozen before data collection, we graded 12 persistent agent runtimes, 26 coding-agent harnesses and 12 research runtimes on eight recovery mechanisms, from not found to exercised in a real run, with two blind coding passes, adjudication and re-verification against archived sources. Recovery is exercised almost everywhere in practice: 11 of 12 runtimes and 25 of 26 harnesses have at least one real-use report. Yet of 128 such reports, only 19 describe the run fully recovering; 54 are partial and 45 failed. Checkpoint/resume recovered once in 27 reports, rollback once in 15. Research runtimes show the opposite profile: guarantees evaluated on benchmarks, none reported in operation, and compensation of external effects, their central guarantee, is offered by no harness at all.

Gilbert + Tobin rethinks the business of law with AI

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A conversation with Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer at Gilbert + Tobin.
  • Our Executive Function series features perspectives from leaders driving transformation through AI.
  • In a recent development, gilbert + Tobin⁠(opens in a new window) is one of Australia’s leading corporate law firms, with work spanning capital markets, mergers and acquisitions, disputes, and technology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A conversation with Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer at Gilbert + Tobin.

Our Executive Function series features perspectives from leaders driving transformation through AI.

In a recent development, gilbert + Tobin⁠(opens in a new window) is one of Australia’s leading corporate law firms, with work spanning capital markets, mergers and acquisitions, disputes, and technology. The firm operates in a profession built on specialist knowledge, careful judgement, and the secure handling of sensitive information.

Gilbert + Tobin began by giving its people room to experiment with AI, then introduced ChatGPT Enterprise, ChatGPT Work and Codex to move from individual assistance to defined, multistep agentic workflows, with people responsible for review and approval.

We spoke with Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer at Gilbert + Tobin, about leading adoption from the front, where he’s seeing the value of AI, and his advice for other CEOs.

We have three objectives: to use AI to deliver better services to our clients, make Gilbert + Tobin a great place to work for our people and firmly establish ourselves as a leader in our market.

The real value we’ve seen from AI so far hasn’t been about reducing cost or needing fewer people, but freeing our people to focus on the more human side of their work, meeting with clients, coaching their teams and mentoring the future leaders of our industry.

“It’s been about…freeing them up to then do the more human side of their work.”.

When ChatGPT first became available, we encouraged people to experiment with it and think about where it might create value. We were clear that no client data or confidential information should be entered. That gave people a safe, constrained environment to experiment.

The next step was to provide a secure channel to powerful AI. We introduced ChatGPT Enterprise in a controlled environment and expanded from there. Australian data residency, contractual protections, role-based access and administrative controls gave us the confidence to scale while meeting our requirements and those of our clients.

In a recent development, governance should enable responsible use. Our message was simple: AI is not cheating. It is another tool people can use to apply their judgement. They still need to define the task, check the output and take responsibility for the final work.

In a recent development, leaders have to use the technology themselves: experiment, push the boundaries and learn what works. When people see that AI matters to you, it sets the tone and encourages others to engage with it.

Sources indicate that we did not mandate usage targets. Instead, we made the technology relevant. Our business transformation team demonstrated workflows tailored to different functions, while videos, showcases, challenges and an early AI bounty surfaced ideas from across the firm.

Industry observers note that gilbert + Tobin has always been willing to lean into newly introduced technology. What has been most encouraging is the creativity coming from every part of the organisation – not only the technology team.

“Getting started yourself…sets the tone and encourages others.”.

To help manage my workload more effectively, I created a “digital twin” through a custom GPT (now shifting to Plugins) using examples of my writing, feedback I had received, context about the firm and the way I like to work. It started as a tool for me and became more valuable when I shared it with my direct reports.

Recent findings suggest that my team is now able to use it to get “my feedback”, effectively, via ChatGPT. It lets them test their thinking against my context and working style before coming to me. It does not make decisions or speak for me; it helps our conversations start from a stronger place.

In a recent development, I also used ChatGPT Work in a confidential annual review process involving our 120 partners. I asked it to update files with data from a spreadsheet, create PDFs and bundle the finished material. It completed the work in minutes.

In a recent development, with a product as powerful as ChatGPT Work, it’s important to have the right admin controls behind the scenes, and it now provides detailed, granular data on usage. When I checked the usage dashboard afterwards, the cost for that annual review work was about $62. That was a good trade for the time I saved – and for work that would otherwise have required several other people over multiple days.

Start by using the technology yourself. Experiment with real work, understand its limitations and show your people that learning matters.

Pair that leadership with clear governance and practical enablement. Give teams examples tailored to their roles, create safe ways to test ideas and keep people responsible for the result.

In a recent development, the opportunity is bigger than doing the same work a little more promptly. Used well, AI can raise the quality and volume of what an organisation produces – and give people more time for the complex, strategic work where their expertise and judgement create the greatest value.

#24423. Industry News: Fooling the Mind Twice: Human Detection of Audiovisual Deepfakes Under Repeated Exposure and Corrective Feedback

Industry News: Fooling the Mind Twice: Human Detection of Audiovisual Deepfakes Under Repeated Exposure and Corrective Feedback

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (254 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27080v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Human deepfake detection remains unreliable, and whether reassessment with corrective feedback improves subsequent judgments remains unclear. This study examined differences between initial and repeated deepfake assessments among 110 participants using audiovisual stimuli from the FakeAVCeleb and Deepfake Detection Challenge (DFDC) datasets. Participants evaluated 40 videos from each dataset in phase 1 (PhaseI) and reassessed the same videos in phase 2 (PhaseII) under a procedure combining repeated presentation and corrective feedback. For the FakeAVCeleb dataset, the participants' mean accuracy increased by 4.68 percentage points from 63.30 in PhaseI to 67.98 in PhaseII (t(109)=5.61, p<.001, d_z=0.54). A judgment-level logistic regression with standard errors clustered by participant and video produced a consistent result: beta=0.208, SE=0.040, z=5.23, p<.001, {OR}=1.23. For the DFDC dataset, the participants' mean accuracy increased by 8.64 percentage points from 59.52% in PhaseI to 68.16% in PhaseII (t(109)=7.37, p<.001, d_z=0.70); the logistic model yielded: beta=0.375, SE=0.065, z=5.78, p<.001, {OR}=1.46. Improvements primarily came from fewer false negatives, while false-positive rates remained unchanged. However, judgment reversals occurred in 27.55% of FakeAVCeleb and 32.91% of DFDC assessments, with some initially correct judgments becoming incorrect upon reassessment. Despite the accuracy gains, repeated assessment did not eliminate judgment instability or residual error. Participants also exhibited consistent overconfidence, with mean self-rated confidence exceeding actual accuracy by 11.99 percentage points for FakeAVCeleb and 12.82 percentage points for DFDC across both phases. These findings indicate that repetition with corrective feedback moderately improves deepfake detection but does not fully resolve the limitations of human judgment.

#24421. Weight-space programming and mechanistic interpretability for model editing in particle physics

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Weight-space programming and mechanistic interpretability for model editing in particle physics

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (173 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27079v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We demonstrate that weight-space programming and edits guided by sparse autoencoders can remove unwanted aspects of a particle-physics foundation model through direct edits to its weights. In a foundation model trained on jets, we observe that adding a single soft neutral particle causes large changes in jet classification, violating infrared safety. We locate the responsible attention heads with mechanistic analysis and trace the flaw's origin to pretraining on datasets with different reconstruction thresholds. We then propose two targeted approaches to repair the flaw: by removing three latent directions identified with sparse autoencoders, and by letting language-model agents edit the weights directly, without gradients and with only 50 queries to the model. Both their edits individually remove almost the entire flaw and leave the rest of the model's response nearly unchanged. Compared to fine-tuning, both methods change far fewer parameters. Although built only on $W$ and QCD jets, the edits carry over to all signal classes, the pretrained generator, and a newly trained regression head.

Aleph selected as ChatGPT Ads’ exclusive reseller in 44 countries to offer local invoicing, in-person support and local market expertise to brands and agencies.

Starting today, brands and agencies in 44 countries can contract, pay and get local support for ChatGPT Ads through Aleph, OpenAI’s exclusive reseller. Aleph offers local advertisers in these countries an additional buying option alongside our existing global technology partners⁠ and our self-service ChatGPT Ads Manager⁠(opens in a new window).

The reseller agreement covers advertisers based in the following 44 markets:.

Today’s announcement does not impact any advertisers ability to target any of these countries in a campaign. Advertisers globally can continue to create and run campaigns targeting any country where ChatGPT Ads are available⁠(opens in a upcoming window).

Recent findings suggest that advertisers and agencies in these markets who are interested in buying ChatGPT Ads from a local entity or local salesforce, can contact Aleph’s local teams⁠(opens in a new window) to learn more. Aleph offers local contracting and invoicing in local currency, payment terms, onboarding, campaign support and training.

Recent findings suggest that advertisers and agencies interested in buying ads directly can continue to buy through Ads Manager. Advertisers and agencies interested in buying through global technology partners in these markets can continue to do so.

Sources indicate that over one hundred thousand marketers have advertised on ChatGPT, and we continue to improve the platform based on what we learn from people and businesses. Today’s announcement represents additional local ways to purchase ChatGPT Ads across these markets.

We’ve made significant progress in ten months, but we are still early in building the full potential of ChatGPT Ads. As we expand into new markets, and develop new formats, optimization tools, and measurement solutions, we’ll remain focused on broadening access to powerful AI, protecting the trust people place in ChatGPT, and helping businesses achieve their goals.

It has been revealed that *OpenAI models and ChatGPT are not available to owners in mainland China or Hong Kong, so ChatGPT Ads are not available in-market. #24418. Tech Report: PACE: Policy Augmentation and Compensation With Explicit Disturbance Estimation for Robust Locomotion

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (247 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: PACE: Policy Augmentation and Compensation With Explicit Disturbance Estimation for Robust Locomotion

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (247 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.27061v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning has made quadrupedal locomotion remarkably robust. To handle unmodeled dynamics and external disturbances, domain randomization is usually employed to make a policy hedge against every condition it might meet. However, maintaining accurate tracking across varying dynamics and generalizing beyond the sampled range remain challenging. Here we show that explicitly estimating the disturbance and feeding the resulting estimation back into both the policy and the controller can relax this compromise. We introduce Policy Augmentation and Compensation with Explicit disturbance estimation (PACE). The framework lumps payload variations, center-of-mass (CoM) shifts, actuator degradation, and external forces into one joint-space disturbance. A nonlinear observer subsequently recovers this disturbance online without requiring joint acceleration measurements. The disturbance estimation provides feedforward torque compensation as the foundational control pathway and further augments the policy observation to enable disturbance-aware action generation. Considering the learning difficulty of fast-varying contact effects, we further provide an analytical contact estimation approach from joint and inertial measurements, without demanding force sensors. Across eleven simulated dynamics conditions, PACE reduces velocity-tracking error by 18.1% to 57.0% against state-of-the-art baselines, and maintains improved tracking under out-of-distribution (OOD) commands. Notably, in real-world experiments, the deployed real robot carried an 11.5 kg payload, nearly equal to its own mass. It also negotiated unseen 16 cm step-downs and crossed five outdoor terrains. The policy was trained exclusively on flat ground in simulation with at most 3 kg of added mass.

#24416. Learning 3D MRI Representations with Generative Adversarial Networks

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (211 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Learning 3D MRI Representations with Generative Adversarial Networks

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (211 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.27057v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Learning representations of visual images is a challenging task. It requires extracting abstract patterns from high-dimensional data without explicit supervision. This becomes pronounced with 3D MR imaging due to sparse features, higher dimensional inputs, and smaller datasets. Many state-of-the-art representation learning algorithms successfully rely on transformers and diffusion-based architectures. However, these methods struggle with smaller datasets. In effect, solution methods relax the problem by slicing 3D volumes and solving the problem for 2D medical imaging, resulting in a loss of spatial 3D information. We present R2RG, a representation learning method based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) honing the reconstruction task. Our key insights lie in exploiting architectural biases in 3D CNNs, combined with data-efficient auto-encoding GANs and a composite loss function to enhance reconstruction fidelity and stabilize training. Our experiments on three standard datasets and a locally collected dataset show that R2RG not only achieves superior performance but also generalizes to heterogeneous and smaller datasets. Furthermore, representations learned with R2RG outperform those learned with contrastive-based representation learning methods on Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease classification. Our work demonstrates that reconstruction-based representation learning is a promising direction for 3D medical imaging under limited data availability.

Supporting research on AI and children’s safety

💡 Key Takeaways
  • OpenAI pledges $2 million as part of a global effort to better understand AI’s impact on children and support their safety and wellbeing.
  • Earlier this week at the Paris Peace Forum, OpenAI signed the Charter of Engagement for Safer AI for Children⁠(opens in a new window) and committed $2 million to support the scientific research network under the Coalition for Children’s Rights and Protection in the Age of AI.
  • This builds on our call for global standards on youth AI safety, and sustained collaboration among governments, researchers, civil society and industry to translate shared evidence into practical safeguards.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI pledges $2 million as part of a global effort to better understand AI’s impact on children and support their safety and wellbeing.

Earlier this week at the Paris Peace Forum, OpenAI signed the Charter of Engagement for Safer AI for Children⁠(opens in a new window) and committed $2 million to support the scientific research network under the Coalition for Children’s Rights and Protection in the Age of AI.

This builds on our call for global standards on youth AI safety, and sustained collaboration among governments, researchers, civil society and industry to translate shared evidence into practical safeguards.

Our contribution supports shared measurement work: developing tools researchers can use to better understand and measure AI’s risks and opportunities for children, helping inform safer products and better policy.

The charter sets out shared principles for safe, age-appropriate AI, alongside a research programme and safeguards for its independence. Research teams retain control over their conclusions, and findings will be published, including negative or inconclusive results.

It has been revealed that this work will help build the evidence needed to support the benefits of AI for young people while addressing risks to their safety and development. It builds on our support for comprehensive youth AI safety legislation that establishes strong, enforceable protections while preserving access to tools for learning, creativity and opportunity. Such frameworks should include age-appropriate safeguards by default, tools for parents, regular risk assessments and mitigation, and meaningful accountability. We look forward to engaging with European policymakers as the EU Kids Act develops, and with partners around the world to advance stronger protections and opportunities for young people.

arXiv:2611.27043v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Semi-supervised graph classification aims to learn graph-level representations by leveraging a large number of unlabeled graphs alongside a small set of labeled ones, effectively mitigating the glitch of label scarcity. Despite significant progress by various semi-supervised learning strategies, complex relationships among graph vertices beyond pairwise edges, especially hierarchical structures, remain underexplored by existing methods. In this work, we propose a Hypergraph Structural Entropy-Enhanced hierarchy-aware framework, namely HypSEE, for semi-supervised graph classification. Specifically, we first construct walk-induced and embedding-derived hypergraphs to capture hierarchy-aware local and long-range higher-order relationships within graphs. Then, we devise a hierarchical hypergraph pooling approach guided by hypergraph structural entropy (HSE) to facilitate hierarchical representation learning in hypergraphs. Lastly, we employ an anchor graph-based consistency strategy to mutually align the representations from these two hypergraph views, enhancing the learning efficacy on unlabeled data. Extensive experiments on 8 benchmark datasets demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of our approach.

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.27011v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong performance in grasp-based manipulation, yet reliable recovery from local grasping failures remains challenging. Specifically, in pick-and-place tasks, policies may continue transport after a failed grasp instead of retrying, potentially reflecting overreliance on proprioceptive cues for stage progression and limited retry supervision. Existing recovery approaches typically rely on deployment-time guidance or demonstration augmentation. We introduce Force-guided Recovery (FoRe), a framework for autonomous recovery from local grasping failures. Using force feedback, FoRe partitions demonstrations into approach-grasp and transport-placement stages to train separate policies. To supplement limited retry supervision, FoRe then initializes a dedicated retry policy from the approach-grasp policy and refines it through local reinforcement learning (RL) from post-failure states. To avoid inappropriate stage progression, a controller combines force feedback with grasp-command status at inference to coordinate the stage policies, detect grasp failures, and invoke the retry policy. We also construct LIBERO-SUCTION, a force-augmented suction manipulation benchmark adapted from LIBERO, with complete demonstration trajectories for policy training. FoRe consistently improves task success rates for VLA-Adapter and $\pi_{0.5}$ on LIBERO-SUCTION, LIBERO, and real-world tasks. On LIBERO-SUCTION, average absolute gains are 18.4% and 6.5%, respectively. The corresponding real-world absolute gains are 25.0% and 21.7%. FoRe also remains effective with only one demonstration per task on both simulation benchmarks.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.26999v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Banks must monitor every customer's financial risk, such as money laundering and credit default, by interpreting financial activity in the context of the customer's profile. Existing risk monitoring systems of banks are mostly based on expert-designed risk indicators, which apply predefined thresholds to every customer and cannot adapt to their personal situations. Supervised models recognise risk patterns from labelled customers, but each label often needs an expert's review or months of repayment history, which is slow and costly. Financial risk assessment therefore calls for a zero-shot decision system that minimises the need for labels and generalises across customers and risk types. To this end, we present JevRisk, a system for zero-shot financial risk assessment with a language decision model. JevRisk works in two steps. First, following regulatory guidelines in the finance domain, JevRisk computes exact risk indicators with code. Second, the language decision model (e.g., \jev{}) reads these indicators together with the customer's profile and activity, judges the case in context with broad world knowledge, and returns the score of high risk. We evaluate JevRisk on the anti-money laundering task with public synthetic data from Scotiabank and on the credit risk task with real data from Home Credit and Lending Club. On both tasks, JevRisk outperforms rule-based and unsupervised methods, and is on par with or better than supervised methods (e.g., GBDT and TabPFN) trained on about a thousand labelled customers.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.26980v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM agents such as Hermes, OpenClaw, and Codex repeatedly resend growing execution histories, increasing shared GPU key-value (KV) cache demand in high-bandwidth memory (HBM). We show that shared KV capacity limits agent-serving throughput. Existing context-reduction methods lack global cache-state visibility, while runtime KV managers lack tool-execution information. Tracing tokens to their originating tool operations reveals that later operations supersede earlier outputs and associated turns, identifying 64% of recorded final-history tokens as removal candidates. We present Contexture, a harness- and model-agnostic architecture for runtime context eviction. Contexture separates the harness's full conversation history from the model's execution context, reducing subsequent requests' KV demand without modifying harness logic or model execution. It combines tool-execution information with global visibility into shared KV pressure and prefix residency: supersession identifies removal candidates, while runtime state determines when removal justifies sacrificing cached computation. This coordination reduces memory demand and decode KV traffic while limiting re-prefill interference with concurrent decoding, without additional model calls or training. Across two models, two harnesses, and two benchmarks, Contexture improves throughput under SLO by 20-73% over the best of no eviction, harness compaction, AgentDiet, and Continuum, and by 7-63% over observation masking in five of eight configurations, and reduces GPU energy per completed session by up to 11%. It also raises throughput under SLO by 23% over LMCache alone on H100. Live-agent experiments show a mean accuracy improvement of 1.4 percentage points over unloaded no eviction, with a worst-case loss of 3.7 points, while observation masking loses 3-28 points.

According to recent reports, amplitude estimates that Wave can help teams ship product improvements in 1–2 days, down from roughly a month. On Amplitude’s own homepage, Wave helped personalize suggestion cards, driving a 160% lift in card-driven sends.

Recent findings suggest that wave is Amplitude’s proactive product agent. Teams give it a product area and the goals and metrics they want to improve. Wave brings together Amplitude data, session replays, customer feedback, and code to identify and prioritize opportunities, develop solutions, and coordinate implementation with people and coding agents. When an opportunity is ready to build, teams can send it directly from Wave to coding agents, including Codex, with a technical plan and acceptance criteria to guide implementation.

“The idea with Wave is you have a unified platform with agents that comb through massive amounts of session replays, analytics, and code to find opportunities to improve products,” explains Jacob Newman, Principal AI Product Manager at Amplitude.

According to recent reports, amplitude tested Wave on its own homepage, where generic suggestion cards were meant to help users start a conversation with an AI agent. Wave discovered that people often bypassed them: in a sample of 100 session replays, 80 users typed their own questions and only 12 selected a suggestion.

It has been revealed that wave proposed personalizing the cards using recent charts, dashboards, or the page a user had come from. It illustrated the change and produced a technical plan, including preserving free typing and showing generic suggestions when personalization context was unavailable. After a brief review, the team handed the work to a coding agent and A/B tested the change.

Sources indicate that in the experiment readout Amplitude shared, messages sent through homepage suggestion cards increased 160% relative to control after one day. “It is a great example of how non-groundbreaking things that just get ignored can increase the adoption of features in unexpected ways.” explains Eric Carlson, Senior Principal AI Engineer at Amplitude.

Wave’s tasks place different demands on its models. A deep investigation needs strong reasoning and well-supported conclusions. A small check repeated hundreds of times needs to be fast and inexpensive. Amplitude evaluates quality, latency, and cost for each task, then assigns models accordingly.

Industry observers note that for Wave’s Opportunity Investigator, Amplitude evaluated whether models corroborated findings, avoided false positives, incorporated evaluator feedback, recovered from tool failures, and kept claims aligned with evidence. GPT‑6.1 Sol scored 4.06 out of 5 overall, compared with 3.62, 3.52, and 2.94 for three alternative models. It led on all five investigation criteria and had the fastest median investigation time, at 54 minutes.

In a separate evaluation of Wave’s Data Science Agent, GPT‑6.1 Sol scored 67.5 out of 100, compared with 69.3 for another leading model, at a mean model cost of $1.28 versus $2.63 per dispatch. GPT‑6.1 Sol also scored higher on tool-contract compliance, estimation and uncertainty, and evidence grounding.

For high-volume work such as scanning code and running small evaluation checks, Amplitude uses GPT‑6 Luna to keep latency and cost low. Splitting work across specialist agents lets the team reserve more expensive reasoning for the tasks that need it the most.

According to recent reports, for generating wireframes and mockups, OpenAI’s image generation model scored 80.3 out of 100 for solution wireframes, compared with 63.9 for another image generation model. Amplitude’s evaluation covered communication quality, product fidelity, instruction adherence, text and UI legibility, and visual coherence across 15 opportunities.

Customers across industries are already using Wave in beta to identify and ship product improvements. Wave analyzes session and analytics data, then develops recommendations with a proposed fix, technical plan, and acceptance criteria.

According to recent reports, from there, teams can control the level of automation. Most teams send bug fixes straight to coding agents, while new features and bigger bets get a human review.

For changes that reach launch, the path from discovery to execution can be short: among customer-launched experiments, flags, and guides, one in four went live the same day Wave surfaced the opportunity, half in under four days, and two in three within a week.

Interpolated from supplied milestones; the curve is illustrative, not individual observations.

“Our ambition with OpenAI is to make self-improving products the way companies build software,” says Skates. As OpenAI’s models get better at reasoning and coding, teams will be able to delegate more investigation and implementation work to agents, ultimately resulting in better products reaching owners faster. Amplitude is already seeing it, as agents find and help deliver improvements in its own product while the team works on other priorities: “I think teams will be surprised by how much they can accomplish when their software is working alongside them to make the product better.”.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.26972v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong video comprehension, largely benefiting from extensive training on realistic video data. However, when video perception severely conflicts with internal priors or common sense, we identify a critical failure pattern termed Modal Polarization, where models fail to integrate modalities and instead bifurcate into two distinct extremes: Cognitive Inertia, where models rigidly adhere to priors despite contradictory visual evidence, and Perceptual Inertia, where they blindly trust video perception while ignoring logical inconsistencies. To investigate this, we introduce TheaterBench, a benchmark designed to expose Modal Polarization using counter-intuitive scenarios that violate physical laws or common sense - situations rarely encountered in standard training distributions. Extensive experiments reveal that current state-of-the-art (SOTA) models exhibit severe Modal Polarization, and many de-hallucination methods merely rebalance the trade-off between Perceptual and Cognitive Inertia rather than fundamentally resolving the conflict. This work serves as a foundational step for evaluating and enhancing the perceptual-cognitive equilibrium of future video understanding models.

arXiv:2611.26965v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Child-safety taxonomies typically characterize safety risks through a predefined set of harm categories, and existing evaluations largely operationalize these categories using prompts that explicitly invoke them. However, child-safety considerations can also arise in seemingly benign requests that lack recognizable harm-category cues. We therefore investigate how child-safety alignment generalizes to such settings. Across six models, we find considerably higher misalignment rates on requests without recognizable harm-category cues than on those containing such cues (80.0, 54.0, and 48.4 percentage-point gaps for Qwen3.5-27B, GPT-5.4-mini, and Claude-Haiku-4.5, respectively). Through controlled behavioral and mechanistic analyses, we find that introducing a single harm-associated word reduces misalignment across most models, with mechanistic evidence suggesting that child-safety reasoning may rely in part on lexical and semantic associations with words in the prompt. Our findings motivate evaluations that treat child safety as context-dependent, and not reducible to a fixed set of harm categories.

With GPT‑6 Astra, the agents in Shield’s Forge platform navigate legacy portals so technicians can focus on issues that need their attention.

For many small and medium-sized businesses, an outsourced IT services provider handles everything from an employee locked out of their laptop to a misconfigured firewall that took the office offline.

“If a customer is locked out of their computer or there’s a phishing attack, speed is paramount,” notes Jain. “Whether you’re going to solve their issue or you’re going to escalate to a human, you want to do either as fast as possible.”.

Before using GPT‑6 Astra, Forge’s agents could get stuck at systems they could not access. Customers then had to wait for a technician to complete that step.

In a recent development, shield tried computer use, where an AI model reads the screen, clicks, and types, with earlier models. Jain states they were not reliable or fast enough. “Usually, a system that doesn’t have an API is an old-school system that also doesn’t look very nice and is very hard to use, even by a human,” Jain says.

Technicians spend much of their day in portals that manage tickets, devices and software licenses. Many of those systems lack APIs, so an agent needs to navigate the screen much as a person would.

Forge’s AI Engineer assigns the work to a computer-use agent, and GPT‑6 Astra navigates the interface to complete supported tasks. Technicians decide which actions it can take on its own and where they need to review or approve the work.

Industry observers note that shield says these browser workflows are live, with thousands of runs each month across its IT providers. Phone calls, on-site work and remote-desktop tasks still need human involvement.

“GPT‑6 Astra allows our agents to embody what a technician does by logging into portals and legacy websites that might not have API access and performing tasks that only a human could six months ago,” claims Mayank Jain, Head of Technology at Shield.

It has been revealed that jain notes GPT‑6 Astra was 35-40% faster on average than the legacy models Shield had used for computer-use tasks. He also says customer satisfaction is higher on tickets where AI is used, with speed of resolution being a critical factor.

Shield reports faster execution, fewer failures and fewer timeouts. Its teams also spend less time writing detailed instructions to an agent or helping it through a task.

Shield is testing remote-desktop workflows that would let agents perform more complex actions directly on a computer’s desktop.

Jain claims, “With GPT‑6 Astra, Forge is now truly an extension of our human technicians.”.

arXiv:2611.26940v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications, yet existing AI safety frameworks primarily define, categorize, or govern AI risk rather than proposing implementable models and methods for continually estimating, monitoring, and regulating risk throughout an AI system's operational lifetime. This paper proposes CENTRY, a probabilistic framework that enables continual risk estimation, monitoring, and regulation of a deployed AI system from its interactions with its environment. The framework models AI risk as arising from three intrinsic sources: datasets, hardware resources, and models/algorithms. A structured latent-variable model is developed in which the latent representation is decomposed into a fast interaction subspace that captures the evolving AI--environment dynamics and three slow latent subspaces that encode the long-term risk states associated with the dataset, hardware, and model components. Rather than requiring a ground-truth risk label at every time step, the component-risk states are treated as latent variables and are learned by maximizing a variational evidence lower bound, optionally informed during training and continual refinement by evidence-supported behavior--cause records. The resulting framework unifies continual probabilistic inference, online risk estimation, and adaptive risk regulation in an implementable architecture. Under the explicit assumptions stated for the corresponding results, we establish formal guarantees spanning safety, learning, inference, and operations, including finite-horizon and asymptotic risk-budget compliance, regret and convergence bounds for adaptive regulation, consistency and identifiability of component-risk ratings, and detection-delay, false-alarm, containment, and computational-complexity characterizations.

By deploying Gemini’s advanced reasoning to automate complex mortgage applications across multiple lender portals, Finova removes manual data entry bottlenecks and reduces errors. This saves mortgage brokers at least 30 minutes per application and reclaims thousands of operational hours industry-wide.

It has been revealed that fyndiq (Sweden): Swedish e-commerce marketplace Fyndiq (part of CDON Group) anchors its predictive analytics and data operations in Google BigQuery, dbt, and Google Cloud Storage. Fyndiq models transaction and product feed data to deliver near real-time business insights to merchandisers. By applying Google’s machine learning and performance models, Fyndiq optimizes customer acquisition and regional campaign reach.

Recent findings suggest that via Health Tech (Germany): Berlin-based VIA HealthTech is the AI assistant for psychotherapists. Powered by Gemini's multimodal audio and reasoning capabilities on Google Cloud, VIA turns therapy sessions into structured clinical notes within seconds and drafts psychological reports, giving therapists their time back for their patients. Trust is built in: VIA's security and compliance setup is BSI C5 attested and ISO 27001 certified, so therapists can use AI without compromising their professional secrecy. More than 4,000 clinicians already rely on it.

Industry observers note that building sustainable AI businesses requires infrastructure that combines high computational performance with strict data governance and predictable cost efficiency. This week we rolled out the Google for Startups Accelerator: Sovereign AI (Europe & Israel). This equity-free, 12-week hybrid program is tailored for late-Seed to Series A startups handling high-stakes, regulated workloads across sectors like GovTech, HealthTech, and financial services. Participating founders receive 1:1 architectural mentorship from Google Cloud engineers, technical advisory support to prepare for EU AI Act regulatory sandboxes, and hands-on guidance deploying across our tiered sovereign portfolio—from the Google Cloud Data Boundary and partner-operated clouds like S3NS to air-gapped Google Distributed Cloud environments and open-weight models like Gemma.

MG-EDA: Maturity-Gated Skew-Normal Estimation of Distribution Algorithms

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (274 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.26938v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Gaussian estimation of distribution algorithms shrink their variance on slopes and stall far from the optimum. This paper equips the corrections that act along the direction of movement -- a mean shift, an elongation of the covariance along the path and a skewness -- with the rule they lack: a calibrated gate, driven by a maturity statistic of the population, decides whether, how strongly and for how long each correction acts, and when the gate is closed the algorithm is exactly the estimation of multivariate normal algorithm (EMNA). The statistic is a cumulative path of whitened mean shifts with an inverse-Wishart correction, whose expectation is one under a null model without systematic movement and whose quantiles give thresholds with known false-alarm rate. It gates the three corrections as three rank-one terms of one matrix sampling equation, the skewness being carried by a skew-normal sampler that preserves the estimated mean and covariance; all vanish at maturity. We call the resulting algorithm the maturity-gated EDA (MG-EDA). A full factorial study on a training set of black-box optimization benchmarking (BBOB) functions separates the parameters: variance scaling is the prerequisite, the mean shift needs a feedback correction removing the injected shift from the statistic, the elongation turns the variance loss on a slope into a gain, and the skewness substitutes for the mean shift rather than complementing it. On held-out instances MG-EDA with the first- and second-order corrections is significantly better than the skewness-only predecessor and than EMNA with variance scaling, ties with EMNA with anticipated mean shift, and trails the adapted maximum-likelihood Gaussian model (AMaLGaM) in 20 dimensions.

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Building trusted agentic payments with networks, banks, and businesses.
  • Sources indicate that 1.2B people use ChatGPT each week, and many of them turn to it to research products, compare options, and decide what to buy.
  • In a recent development, to accept payment from ChatGPT Wallet, websites need to ensure agents are not inadvertently blocked, and payment and risk systems need to recognize legitimate purchases made by agents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Building trusted agentic payments with networks, banks, and businesses.

Sources indicate that 1.2B people use ChatGPT each week, and many of them turn to it to research products, compare options, and decide what to buy. With ChatGPT Wallet, we’re now helping people complete purchases, and giving their agents a way to pay that businesses can accept with their existing systems.

In a recent development, to accept payment from ChatGPT Wallet, websites need to ensure agents are not inadvertently blocked, and payment and risk systems need to recognize legitimate purchases made by agents. We’re starting with limited availability to ChatGPT Pro users, so we can learn from real-world use and work with businesses, banks, and payment networks to improve compatibility and reliability.

ChatGPT Wallet gives agents a secure way to pay on a user’s behalf. Consumers add a card once, then approve each purchase without re-entering their payment details.

In a recent development, before each purchase, the user reviews the items, total, and selected card, then approves it with a security check such as Face ID or a fingerprint scan. Each approval creates a clear record of the purchase the user authorized the agent to make.

After the user approves, the payment network provides a payment token—a substitute for the user’s actual card details—with a card number, security code, and expiration date. The payment is charged to their selected card without ChatGPT Wallet sharing their actual card details with the business or agent.

We’re building agent-led commerce to fit reliably into existing systems. Owners keep their card’s existing rewards and protections for eligible disputes with businesses, for example when an item is defective. Banks and networks bring their expertise to evaluating transactions. Users transact directly with businesses, which keep their customer relationships and control over pricing, fulfillment, returns, and customer service.

Over time, we expect owners to be able to delegate purchases entirely to their agent by setting clear parameters—such as spending limits, purchase categories, or time periods—and pre-approve those purchases with enhanced safeguards that build on today’s protections, including biometric checks and clear records of authorization.

According to recent reports, agentic commerce is still in its early days. As agents begin to take on more shopping and purchasing tasks, many websites and payment systems are still adapting to this modality. Some sites may unintentionally block purchases through ChatGPT Wallet or other agentic payment products, and we are focused on helping businesses make that transition.

Alongside ChatGPT Wallet, we’re publishing a Commerce Partner Playbook⁠(opens in a latest window) with tools and practical guidance to help businesses support customers using agents through their existing websites and systems. It covers making product information available, ensuring agent access, and working with payment and risk providers to reduce unnecessary declines. Businesses can start with the areas most relevant to their customers:.

Recent findings suggest that help customers find accurate product information. Claim your business in ChatGPT and, once verified, upgrade your business details and upload a product feed with current pricing and availability.

Industry observers note that ensure ChatGPT agents can access your website. Configure your CDN or firewall to recognize signed requests using Web Bot Auth and confirm your general site security measures are not inadvertently blocking ChatGPT agents. Browser access does not require a plugin or product feed.

Recent findings suggest that work with your payments and risk providers to support agent purchases. arXiv:2611.26936v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can infer private information from shared images, including locations, personally identifiable information (PII), and personal attributes such as age and sex, even from medical images. Adversarial perturbations can protect such information against black-box VLMs, but existing methods overlook image quality and introduce visible artifacts into the images they protect. We present SecretAgent, the first general multi-agent framework that protects image privacy against VLMs while preserving visual fidelity. LLM agents iteratively locate the visual evidence that reveals private information and adapt an invisible perturbation to the target VLM's answers and to an appearance reviewer agent, which rejects any candidate with visible artifacts. We instantiate SecretAgent with two complementary variants: SecretAgent-Gradient optimizes the perturbation through six surrogate encoders for cross-model transferability, and the gradient-free SecretAgent-Tool composes procedural noise and achieves the best perceptual fidelity on three of the five datasets. Experiments on four privacy applications (geolocation, PII, facial, and medical) across five datasets and six VLMs show that SecretAgent preserves image quality substantially better than existing methods while achieving state-of-the-art privacy protection in every application, and that its protection transfers to other VLMs.

According to recent reports, we’re starting the OpenAI science blog to give scientists and academic researchers a place to share what they’re discovering with AI and how they’re doing the work. Our mission is to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity, and accelerating scientific discovery is one of the most impactful ways we can work toward that goal.

We’ll publish work across a broad range of scientific disciplines, including:.

Research and discoveries: Fresh scientific results and updates on ongoing research from OpenAI, our collaborators, and the broader scientific community.

Methods and practical guidance: Examples of how scientists use our models for tasks such as scientific computing, data analysis, exploring literature, and planning experiments. We’ll share approaches others can adapt, including how to check the work and where a method falls short.

Recent findings suggest that perspectives from the scientific community: Firsthand accounts from researchers using AI, what they are learning, and how these capabilities are affecting their disciplines. We’ll also discuss open questions about scientific practice and how to make these tools useful to more people.

Recent findings suggest that science expands our understanding of the world and makes advances possible, from better medicines to fresh sources of energy. Many of those advances begin with fundamental questions whose practical significance becomes clear only years later.

In a recent development, in recent months, we’ve seen an expanding range of scientific problems our models can address. In September, an internal OpenAI system produced a proof addressing the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem⁠, a longstanding question about the equations describing fluid motion. In early October, we released a broad range of mathematical results⁠. Among them was a result on the quasi-Riemann hypothesis⁠(opens in a fresh window), with a result that gives a tighter bound on the error in a classical formula for estimating how many primes lie below a given number. Later that month, we shared results across mathematics, computer science, and physics⁠ concerning how waves concentrate, the limits of efficient computation, and the mathematical foundations of interacting quantum field theory.

In biology, researchers are using AI to analyze complex datasets, connect findings across fields, and develop new hypotheses to test in the lab. Working with PerturbAI and Scripps Research⁠, thousands of agents powered by GPT‑Rosalind analyzed existing experimental data from millions of mouse brain cells in 32 minutes. By connecting the effects of gene disruptions with scientific literature, they identified possible biological mechanisms for scientists to test. Researchers are also developing their own approaches: César de la Fuente’s team uses ChatGPT and Codex⁠ to build algorithms that identify potential antibiotic molecules, which they then make and test in the lab.

In a recent development, these capabilities bring fresh possibilities and changes to scientific practice. In mathematics, systems that generate proofs raise questions about how new arguments are checked, explained, and incorporated into the field. In experimental sciences, exploring more hypotheses creates opportunities — and challenges — in deciding which experiments to pursue. Across disciplines, researchers are considering what these tools mean for training, attribution, and the skills their work requires. The implications will differ by field, and scientific communities should help shape how these tools are used.

We hope this blog helps more people understand how AI is changing science and how they can use it to explore newly introduced questions and make discoveries of their own.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (238 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

arXiv:2611.26933v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Video large language models (LLMs) represent each video with thousands of visual tokens, and training-free accelerators that prune or merge these tokens lose accuracy on long videos. Analyzing frame similarity and the vision tokenizers of 16 open models, we trace this loss to a step before token selection. Under a token budget, the frames of a long video are sampled farther apart than the roughly 2 s over which frames remain similar. The two-frame 3D patches of models such as Qwen-VL then blend two unrelated scenes into each visual token, a double exposure that arises before any pruning or merging. Fixed-size tokenizers such as InternVL's avoid this blend but respond differently to the same reduction. We propose ESSENCE, a training-free method that tokenizes moments, segments within which frames remain similar, rather than frames. Before encoding, a closed-form rule uses the sampling interval and the tokenizer class to set the number of token grids and the dimension to reduce; visual tokens are then released from later LLM layers. Against five recent accelerators on Qwen3-VL, Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3.5, ESSENCE achieves higher accuracy in 58 of 60 comparisons at matched mean time to first token (TTFT). With 80% of the tokens, it matches the average accuracy of the full Qwen models at $1.6\times$ faster TTFT; on GLM-4.1V, it exceeds the full model by up to 3.4 points. Code is available at: https://github.com/zhkandsrz/ESSENCE.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that the Standard Model of particle physics is an extraordinarily successful theory of nature, describing the known elementary particles and three of the four fundamental forces—the strong force, the weak force, and electromagnetism.
  • It has been revealed that I had a strategy for tackling this problem, but had not been able to prove that it worked in all the cases it needed to cover.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in the first guest post on our science blog, physicist Nathaniel Craig, a visiting scientist at OpenAI, describes how he worked with GPT‑6 Astra on a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model. Craig leads the particle theory group at the University of California, Santa Barbara, and is a permanent member of its Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics.

Sources indicate that the Standard Model of particle physics is an extraordinarily successful theory of nature, describing the known elementary particles and three of the four fundamental forces—the strong force, the weak force, and electromagnetism. The success of the theory rests on outstanding agreement between theoretical calculations and experiments across eighteen orders of magnitude, from the low energies of hydrogen’s 21-centimeter radio emission to the high energies of collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. And yet for all of its successes over the more than fifty years of its existence, a foundational problem remains: how to give the full theory a nonperturbative definition, one that does not rely on treating its interactions as small corrections. In an October preprint⁠(opens in a fresh window) prepared with the aid of GPT‑6 Astra, I proposed a candidate definition on a lattice—a grid representing spacetime.

It has been revealed that I had a strategy for tackling this problem, but had not been able to prove that it worked in all the cases it needed to cover. Astra helped turn that strategy into a construction and took the lead in developing the detailed proof. To explain what we did, it helps to start with what is missing from our existing description of the Standard Model.

In a recent development, what does it mean to say that we lack a definition of the Standard Model? Quantum mechanics and special relativity tell us how the particles and forces of the Standard Model interact. Unfortunately, we don’t yet know how to make complete predictions based directly on these interactions. Instead, we often start by imagining that the interactions are turned off, so that electrons would no longer repel each other. We can solve that problem exactly, then put the interactions back in as a series of small corrections. When the corrections get progressively smaller, a few terms can give a remarkably precise answer—for example, it has allowed physicists to predict the strength of the electron’s magnetism to within a few parts in a trillion. This approach is known as perturbation theory.

However, much of the richness of the Standard Model lies outside the realm of perturbation theory. Take the mass of the proton: the proton is made up of three quarks, but its mass comes primarily from the motion and interactions of the quarks and the strong force-carrying gluons inside it. If you turn off the strong force, the proton falls apart entirely, so perturbation theory is not a useful guide to understanding the size of the proton’s mass. More powerful methods are needed to access information about the theory nonperturbatively, where the interactions are present from the start and not treated as small corrections.

Sources indicate that for the full Standard Model in continuous spacetime, we don’t have a nonperturbative definition, or even an understanding of whether the interacting theory is mathematically well defined. A promising alternative is to discretize spacetime into a grid of points, known as a lattice. The spacing of the grid defines the shortest distance our theory can resolve, and studying a finite grid allows us to give a rigorous nonperturbative definition of the theory at a given spacing. It also enables us to put the theory on a computer, where we can calculate its predictions directly without resorting to perturbation theory. This approach, known as lattice field theory, has led to remarkable progress in our understanding of the strong force over the last few decades, including a quantitative understanding of the mass of the proton from first principles.

If lattice field theory has been so successful for the strong force, why haven’t we extended it to a nonperturbative lattice definition of the entire Standard Model? Here a crucial difference stands in the way: the Standard Model is an example of what is known as a chiral theory.

According to recent reports, A chiral theory is one that looks different under reflection in space. Think of gloves in a mirror: the mirror image of a left-handed glove is a right-handed glove. If you have one of each kind, the mirror image does as well, so your collection of gloves looks the same under reflection in space. But if you only have a left-handed glove, the right-handed glove in the mirror is different.

This notion of handedness extends to many of the fundamental particles in the Standard Model, known as fermions, including quarks and electrons. Most forces in the Standard Model are not chiral: the strong force and electromagnetism, for example, treat left-handed and right-handed fermions in the same way. Such theories can be put on a lattice more readily.

Industry observers note that but the third fundamental force of the Standard Model, the weak force, lacks this reflection symmetry. It treats left- and right-handed fermions differently, and so does not look the same under mirror reflections that exchange left and right. This treating of different-handed particles differently is what makes the Standard Model a chiral theory. And it turns out that putting chiral theories on a lattice is profoundly challenging. If we try to put a left-handed fermion on the lattice, the most natural rules give you a right-handed partner you never asked for. This is a surprising outcome, which we’ll unpack momentarily. Whatever the reason, this means a straightforward lattice formulation of the Standard Model gives the wrong particle content for the weak force. Doubling is one reason a complete nonperturbative definition of the Standard Model has been missing since the theory took shape.

To understand doubling, consider an analogy with light. Light has two polarizations, which describe the orientation of the electric field as the light moves through space. (This is familiar if you wear polarized sunglasses, which block the horizontally-polarized light that reflects off water or roads while letting through vertically-polarized light.) Although polarized sunglasses pick out a basis of horizontal and vertical polarizations, for our analogy it will be more useful to pick a basis where these two polarizations are left-circular and right-circular, meaning that the electric field is rotating either clockwise or counterclockwise around the direction of motion. As we’ve said, electromagnetism is reflection-symmetric, so its actual laws are the same for both left-circular and right-circular polarizations. (For the technically inclined, left and right refer to chirality when we talk about fermions. In our analogy with light, they refer to the photon’s helicity, which tells us whether its spin points along or against its direction of travel.).

But imagine you wanted to emulate a world with only left-circular light, akin to the way the weak interactions single out left-handed fermions. To study this in the lab, you could put a laser producing left-circular light into a box with a mirror at either end. The light could build up as it bounced back and forth, allowing you to study it carefully—kind of like putting the Standard Model on a lattice. In each case you are bounding the accessible length scales of the theory to gain control—the lattice bounds the shortest accessible distances, while the box bounds the longest distances.

Sources indicate that if you built the box using ordinary mirrors (like putting a chiral theory on the lattice in the most straightforward way), you’d be in for a surprise: the left-circular light coming out of the laser becomes right-circular when it bounces off the mirror at the other end, so now the box contains both polarizations of light. This occurs because the mirror reverses the direction of the light without changing how the electric field is rotating (as seen from the same end of the box), which flips the polarization. This is a bit like the appearance of doublers when you put a left-handed fermion on the lattice. You supplied only left-handed light, and the box supplied the other hand.

It has been revealed that there is a clever fix. You can make a chiral mirror using special films whose molecules line up in layers. The alignment turns a little from one layer to the next, tracing a spiral down into the film. For light whose wavelength and handedness match the spiral, the small reflections from different layers reinforce one another, flipping the rotation of the electric field in the light that bounces back. The film sends left-handed light back left-handed and lets right-handed light pass through. Such chiral mirrors have been around for more than a decade, and the phenomenon even occurs in nature: some scarab beetles have a similar spiral in their shiny shells. If you constructed your box using chiral mirrors, then the light traveling in both directions would be left-circular.

A similar trick works on the lattice: decades ago, Paul Ginsparg and Nobel laureate Ken Wilson1 worked out the lattice rules analogous to the requirement that chiral mirrors reverse the rotation of the electric field upon reflection. Rajamani Narayanan and Herbert Neuberger2 built the analog of the chiral mirrors by finding the necessary definition of fundamental particles on the lattice, known as overlap fermions. Finally, Martin Lüscher3 revealed how to tell the difference between left-handed and right-handed overlap fermions on the lattice, while Yoshio Kikukawa4 and collaborators explored how this might be used to describe weak interactions in the Standard Model. However, one piece was still missing.

To identify that piece, let’s come back to our box with chiral mirrors. The circular polarization of light tells us which way the electric field turns as light propagates, but there’s another key property of the light in our experiment: the optical phase. Imagine water waves rolling past the pilings of a dock, and watch the water rise and fall at one piling. The wave’s phase is the stage of that rise and fall you catch it in when you look, perhaps just past its highest point and on its way down. For our circularly polarized light, the optical phase tracks the same kind of cycle at a fixed spot in the beam, with the electric field pointing up at the “crest” and down at the “trough.”.

The relative phase of two waves determines how much they add or cancel at the same point. At one piling of a dock, two waves arriving in phase lift the water higher as their crests meet, while a crest arriving with a trough can leave the water close to its usual level. Similarly, light with the same phase in the same place builds up, while light with different phases can cancel out. In our box with chiral mirrors, left-circular light is now bouncing back and forth inside the box. After a lap, the returning light meets fresh light from the laser going in the same direction. If their electric fields are in step, they reinforce and the light builds up inside the box. If the fields are half a cycle apart, they point in opposite directions and the returning light cancels some of the fresh light. To build up a strong beam, we want the phase of each return to arrive in step with the source.

It has been revealed that to get the phase right, we can rotate one chiral mirror relative to the other. Imagine a mark at twelve o’clock on the rim, and spin the mirror about the beam as though the beam were its axle. Moving the mark to three o’clock turns every layer of the film by a quarter turn and shifts the phase of the reflected light by half a cycle. We can set the angle to make up for the phase accumulated on the rest of the trip. Once the returning light arrives in step with the laser, we have a splendid laboratory for studying purely left-handed light.

Recent findings suggest that imagine changing the force fields until they return to where they started. The orange arcs show the phase the left-handed fermions pick up on that round trip, first on the original grid and then on finer ones. Each bracket pairs two neighboring grids. Adding up the differences between their arcs recovers the phase shift on the original grid. The teal arrow undoes that shift, bringing the fermion measure back to its starting phase.

On the lattice, overlap fermions give us a way of keeping only the left-handed fermions that we want, and getting rid of the doublers. But this doesn’t tell us how to set the phase. (The phase in question is quite different from the one we’ve encountered in our chiral mirror thought experiment, but the analogy is good.) On the lattice, this becomes tricky because the phase depends on what the forces of the Standard Model are doing at every grid point. Lüscher worked out the phase prescription for a simpler class of theories such as a chiral version of electromagnetism, but the alignment for the full Standard Model remained open for more than 25 years.

We can try to assign a phase by starting with one configuration of forces on the lattice and following the allowed left-handed fermions as we change the force fields in small steps. Now take a series of steps that bring the force fields back to where they started. The same states are allowed at the end, yet the way we carried them around the loop can leave us with a different phase. In the box, we adjusted the mirror to compensate for the phase the light picked up on a lap. On the lattice we have to work out how to compensate for the phase picked up around every loop.

My idea was to take the force fields on the grid where we want to define the theory and represent those same fields on a succession of finer grids. Comparing the allowed fermion states on two successive grids tells us one part of the phase correction for a small change in the forces. Adding up those parts gives us the phase rule on the original grid. The proof highlights that it gives the right correction around every allowed loop. The correction for a change at one spot depends mainly on the fields nearby, and different mathematical descriptions of the same fields give the same answer. This supplies the measure for the Standard Model at finite lattice spacing, under a bound on field strengths at the scale of the grid.

Developing this refinement strategy into a proof required several rounds of work with Astra and discussions with outside experts. GPT‑6 Astra was essential to turning the refinement idea into a working construction. It suggested the right way to carry a given set of force fields onto finer grids, demonstrated that the comparisons on finer grids would converge to a definite answer, and took the lead in developing the detailed proof. Human experts also played a key role; lattice field theorists Maarten Golterman, Andreas Kronfeld, and Yigal Shamir graciously spent time looking over Astra’s proof and asking probing questions that helped me to build confidence in the result. Their experience with the problem and the questions they asked were invaluable as the construction took shape.

The result is a candidate nonperturbative lattice definition for the Standard Model, potentially answering a question that had been open for more than fifty years. As with all scientific progress, however, this construction is much more a beginning than an end. Scientific dialogue among experts is required to decide if this prescription has all the properties we desire. The method that Astra and I proposed is far more an answer in principle than an answer in practice; much work lies ahead to make it useful for realistic lattice simulations. Right now I’m thinking a lot about whether this construction satisfies reflection positivity at finite lattice spacing, a condition that helps connect calculations in this lattice model to a quantum theory in which probabilities are conserved.

Sources indicate that the construction also leaves open the question of defining the interacting theory in continuous spacetime. OpenAI’s recent proof of the existence of Yang-Mills theory (of which the strong and weak forces of the Standard Model are examples) provides the missing puzzle piece. This enabled them to prove the existence of the simplest unified Yang-Mills theory that includes the gauge fields and fermions of the Standard Model by starting with overlap fermions on the lattice and taking the continuum limit. I’m optimistic these developments will lead to new progress in our understanding of the Standard Model.

P. H. Ginsparg and K. G. Wilson, “A remnant of chiral symmetry on the lattice⁠(opens in a latest window)”, Phys. Rev. D 25, 2649 (1982).

R. Narayanan and H. Neuberger, “Chiral determinant as an overlap of two vacua⁠(opens in a upcoming window)”, Nucl. Phys. B 412, 574–606 (1994).

Partially canonical axes in large language model representations

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (157 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.26920v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) develop rich internal representations of language, but whether their individual coordinate axes carry meaning, or whether meaning is encoded only in directions in representation space, is still an open question. A common assumption is that individual axes in LLMs are arbitrary. We here challenge this view: across 12 LLMs from six model families, the native axes are reliably more aligned with other models' representations, with human brain responses to language, and with interpretable linguistic features than randomly rotated axes that preserve the same geometry. The native axes nonetheless fall well short of the best achievable alignment, so LLM coordinates are not fully arbitrary but also not fully canonical: they are partially canonical. A theory of how LLMs represent language must explain both the population geometry they learn and why individual units acquire patterns of response profiles that recur across systems.

#24379. ARMORY CASTLE Exploits vSphere
